name: Omar Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Ashby Grange for the Kerr family. It's 120 dairy goats, the milk goes to a cheesemaker, plus wheat and field beans. I start at seven, help Fiona Kerr with the goats, then it's fencing, greasing the machinery, mucking out, fixing whatever's broken. Duncan, her dad, is 64 and slowly handing over to her.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was caretaker at Ashby Primary for twenty-four years. When it merged with the school in the next town in 2023 they only needed one caretaker, and it wasn't me. I was 55 and good with my hands, and Duncan needed someone, so I said yes. Three years on I can fix a fence in my sleep but I still can't tell when a goat's about to kid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing things, same as at the school. I like the goats too, they've got opinions. What wears me out is lifting the feed sacks and being the beginner at my age. My wife Lena does the books for small businesses in town, part-time, and lately she's been losing clients to accounting software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with things. At Ashby Grange I'd say the goats don't care about AI anyway. I'm on one family group chat and that's it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job's fine, but Lena's isn't, even in the quiet version. The routine bookkeeping is exactly the kind of thing that gets automated, and two of her clients already went to an app last year. Her money is about a third of ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Ashby the same as now. We'd put an extra fifty a month aside, just in case Lena loses another client. And I'd tell Lena to start offering something the app can't, like sitting down with the farmers and sorting their messy shoeboxes of receipts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mine's steady, but it's on my mind for Lena. Two of my wife Lena's bookkeeping clients already left her for an app, and nobody called that a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lena think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena is more worried than she lets on. She's 57 and she's done the same books for some clients for twenty years, so she feels betrayed when they go. I try to be cheerful but I count the clients with her every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Lena lost half her clients, what would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The caravan holiday, first. Then probably the second car, because I can cycle to Ashby in summer. We'd keep the heating on; I'm not doing that again like the winter after the school job went.

I'm only on one **family group chat**, so I wouldn't say much online.
think: My job's fine, but Lena's **bookkeeping** is the routine work that gets automated.
Lena's pay is about **a third** of ours, and two clients already left for an app.
do: Keep working at **Ashby Grange** the same as now.
Put an extra **fifty a month** aside in case Lena loses another client.
Encourage Lena to offer **hands-on help** with farmers' receipts that an app can't do.
feel: **Uneasy**: my work feels steady, but **Lena's income** is on my mind.
S0.quote: Two of my wife Lena's bookkeeping clients already left her for an app, and nobody called that a revolution.
fieldNote: Even AI Plateau touches the household through **Lena's routine bookkeeping**.

He is practical: he thinks in **cuts and fixes**, not big plans.

steps.text: Keep doing fencing, machinery and goats at Ashby Grange
Put an extra 50 a month aside for Lena's lost clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs that'll feel it first, and we'd better help people move. At Ashby I'd tell Fiona it's a good time to sort the paperwork side. Online, still not much, maybe a comment on the town page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, Lena's work would shrink by half or more in a few years. Writing, checking, booking, that's her whole job. Mine is mostly hands-on so it's slower, though Fiona would use AI to plan feed and breeding, and she might decide she needs one fewer pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing handyman jobs at weekends for the holiday cottages up the valley, maybe two hundred a month. I'd ask Fiona to show me the goat-health app properly, so I'm more use to her. And we'd put that extra cottage money straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Lena's income going is real, and I'm the junior at Ashby. But I can see a way through, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the holiday cottages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cottages always need a dripping tap fixed or a gate rehung, and the owners live in the city. I did that kind of job every day at the school. A robot won't rehang a holiday cottage gate in the rain for a long while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Fiona might need one fewer pair of hands. Who would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me, honestly, or young Callum who does three days. Callum is quicker with the goats but I'm better with the machines. I'd want to be the one who knows the new app, so I'm harder to let go.

I'd tell Fiona it's a good time to **sort the paperwork** side with AI.

Put the cottage money straight into **savings**.
feel: **Anxious**, as Lena's income goes and I'm the junior at Ashby.
**Steadier** because I can see a way through.
S1.quote: A robot won't rehang a holiday cottage gate in the rain for a long while yet.
fieldNote: **Lena's job** is in the direct line of Steady Disruption, making the household exposed now.
His answer is a **side income** using caretaker skills.
He sees learning the app as **job protection** against Callum.

steps.text: Start weekend handyman jobs at the valley holiday cottages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going far too fast and the government needs to make the companies pay for the fallout. At Ashby I'd say we'll all need a plan. I might even go to a public meeting, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 Lena's bookkeeping is gone, full stop; an AI does the whole year's accounts in a minute. Then in 2031 I'm 63 and a robot can grease, fence and feed. Both our incomes, gone inside three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut the caravan and the second car and put the money aside. I'd build up the cottage handyman work as fast as I can, because that's the last bit robots reach. And I'd look at taking my small council pension from the school early at 60, even with the cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It would keep me awake. I've been through one job going; two at once, with Lena's too, is a different thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night it sank in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been poor before and we managed, and this time at least we see it coming. When my caretaker job went, my wife Lena and I sat in our coats in the kitchen to save on heating. I'd promise her we wouldn't do that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Those three years between the AI and the robots, how would you use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every hour Fiona gives me and every weekend at the cottages. I'd squirrel it all away. By 2031 I'd want a year's money in the bank, which means doubling what we have.

I might even go to a **public meeting**, which I've never done.

S2.quote: When my caretaker job went, my wife Lena and I sat in our coats in the kitchen to save on heating.
fieldNote: Both household incomes fall inside the **three-year window**: Lena's first, his after.
Memory of **sitting in coats** after his caretaker job shapes the fear.
He'd use the gap to **double savings** to a year's cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get people retrained if we start now. At Ashby I'd say let's be sensible and plan. Online I'd share a few practical things for people Lena's age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's work goes in 2031 when she's 62, which is early but not a disaster. Robots in 2034 means I'm 66, so I'd have the state pension. It's tight for those three years, but it's a slope, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Ashby as normal. I'd do the cottage work most weekends and save it, maybe two thousand a year. And I'd help Lena find something hands-on for her last years, maybe the cheese dairy's front shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, because Lena's income goes before she's ready. But it's manageable, with time to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lena go for a job in the cheese shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena loves people, so maybe. She's always said the best bit of bookkeeping is the cup of tea with the client. My wife Lena could sell cheese better than any machine, because she remembers everyone's children's names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the five years change how you feel about Fiona's plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Fiona would have time to tell me straight. I'd ask her outright whether she wants me till 66, and I think she'd say yes if I'm good with the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run and nobody should be caught out. At Ashby I'd say it's Callum's generation that needs to think about it. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's work goes when she's 67, so she'll have retired. I'm retired by 2039 for sure. The thinking AI in 2036 might change how Fiona runs things, but I'll be 68 and gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Ashby and get properly good with the goat-health app, because it'll make Fiona's life easier. I'd keep the cottage work going as a hobby. That's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a bit, about Lena's clients drifting off before then. Mostly it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young Callum to get his welding ticket and learn to fix the robots. Somebody always has to fix the thing that fixes everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not lifting feed sacks at 65, if the machines come early enough. I'd like that very much.

It's **Callum's generation** that needs to think about it.
think: Lena and I will both be **retired** before the change reaches us.
The **2036** AI may change how Fiona runs things, but I'll be gone.
do: Carry on at Ashby and get good with the **goat-health app**.
Keep the **cottage work** going as a hobby.
feel: Mildly **uneasy** about Lena's clients drifting off, but mostly fine.
S4.quote: Somebody always has to fix the thing that fixes everything else.
fieldNote: A decade's warning **clears both** their retirements.
The **existing drift** of Lena's clients to apps still nags.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lena and I would both lose our work inside three years. What would help is a proper retraining grant for people our age, not just young ones. And letting me take my small pension early without a big cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the wives and husbands. Everyone asks about the farmer, but in our house it's Lena's job that goes first. In my house the AI comes for my wife's bookkeeping long before any robot comes for my fences.

headlineQuote: In my house the AI comes for my wife's bookkeeping long before any robot comes for my fences.
portrait: Omar is a **58-year-old** farmhand at Ashby Grange, a former school caretaker who lost that post in a merger.
His wife Lena's **bookkeeping work** is the household's first exposure, even in AI Plateau.
Steady with tech, he'd learn the **goat-health app** and build a weekend handyman side income.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, when both incomes would go within three years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his and Lena's work would both go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining grant** for older workers and drawing his small pension **early** without a big cut.
